question: Despite the local and regional authorities’ opposition1 to the construction of two luxury tourist resorts in Ostuni (Province of Brindisi) and Loiri Porto San Paolo (Province of Gallura NorthEast Sardinia), Italy’s Special Economic Zone (SEZ) mission structure has intervened by issuing single authorisations No 423/20252 (which approved an amended version of Ostuni Council’s development plan for the Mogale district) and No 74/2026 (which, though it gave the go-ahead to the Tavolara Bay project in Loiri Porto San Paolo, has since been revoked as a result of the local council’s decision to withdraw its authorisation).

The notices published by the Official Gazette of the Apulia Region (BURP) specify that, in addition to definitively giving the green light to the amended Mogale district development plan, single authorisation No 423/2025 also deferred the related environmental impact assessment (EIA) to the final design phase (which precedes the issuing of the building permit), even though it had already confirmed that the project’s building type complied with regulations and endorsed the resort’s site and massing provisions and its aesthetic and construction arrangements3.

Article 2(1) of Directive 2011/92/EU requires projects that are likely to have a significant impact on the environment to be assessed prior to approval. Article 2(2) states that EIAs can be integrated into national procedures, but not in such a way as to deprive them of their preventive function. In the light of the above, I ask the Commission to clarify: 1.
Whether postponing the EIA of a project whose essential layout and related townplanning variants have already been approved is an approach that is in line with Directive 2011/92/EU?
Whether SEZ proceedings have the power to amend urban planning arrangements before the completion of the related EIA?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.9.2026) Any project falling within the scope the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive1 and likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue, inter alia, of its nature, size or location, shall be made subject to an assessment before authorisation2.

Where Member States chose to apply a streamlined (joint or coordinated) procedure for assessments of the environmental impacts of a given project arising from two or more Directives, such a procedure shall comply with the obligations under these Directives.

In addition, the Court of Justice of the EU has clarified that Article 2(1) of the EIA Directive requires an environmental impact assessment to be carried out if, in the case the granting of development consent comprises more than one stage, it becomes apparent, in the course of the second stage, that the project is likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue inter alia of its nature, size or location3.

Urban planning is a Member States’ competence. Nevertheless, the adoption or authorisation of any plans, programmes or projects related to urban planning must comply with the provisions of all applicable EU legislation, including those of the Strategic Environmental Assessment Directive4.

It is primarily for the national administrative and judicial authorities to ensure that EU environmental law is correctly applied. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission will monitor the application of the provisions of EU law and may decide to take appropriate action if systemic problems arise5.
